sections.h2: How did Millcreek, Utah become a city?
sections.html:
Millcreek became a city on December 28, 2016, after voters approved incorporation on November 3, 2015. Before that it was a county township, and an earlier incorporation vote in 2012 failed with about 40 percent support.

Salt Lake County created Millcreek Township in 2002 to give residents more say over local planning and to head off annexation by neighboring cities. The first mayor and council were elected in 2016, and the incorporation was recorded at 9:30 a.m. on the December date. Millcreek's own city offices are therefore only a few years old.

sections.h2: Where is Millcreek, and how is it divided?
sections.html:
Millcreek lies between Salt Lake City and South Salt Lake on the north and Murray and Holladay on the south, at about 4,285 feet in elevation. Mill Creek Canyon rises directly to the east.

The city has four community councils, and each covers a distinct part of town.

  • Canyon Rim, in the northeast, has steeper ground.
  • East Mill Creek sits near the mouth of Mill Creek Canyon.
  • Mount Olympus takes in the Olympus Cove area in the eastern foothills.
  • The Millcreek area covers the western and central parts, which are the most densely developed.

Five ZIP codes cover the city: 84106, 84107, 84109, 84117 and 84124. A mailing address alone does not tell you whether a house is in Millcreek, so check the parcel record.

sections.h2: What is the history behind Millcreek's neighborhoods?
sections.html:
Millcreek was settled in 1848 and stayed largely rural until after World War II, when suburban building spread south from Salt Lake City. By the 1980s most of the area was built out.

The area was never annexed, so it was known by names such as East Mill Creek, Canyon Rim and Mount Olympus instead of one city name. The 2000 census counted 30,377 people in the Millcreek census-designated place. The 2010 census merged four such places, and the count rose to 62,139.

Much of the housing therefore went up between the postwar years and the 1980s. On a house that age, the roof, plumbing and wiring are the items an inspector will look at first.

sections.h2: Which parts of Millcreek carry earthquake, slope and flood rules?
sections.html:
Millcreek has a sensitive lands ordinance aimed at faults, liquefaction areas, steep slopes and the Mill Creek floodplain. A city staff presentation on the ordinance (case ZT-23-011) lists those along with avalanche and rockfall zones, alluvial fans, stream corridors, ridgelines and the wildland and urban interface.

The presentation says fault lines and setbacks, Mill Creek floodplains and moderate or high liquefaction areas are all part of the city, and that Mount Olympus debris flow areas roughly match slopes steeper than 30 percent. It describes a fault survey for fault areas, more soils study for liquefaction areas, and a slope analysis and buildable area test for steep ground such as Canyon Rim.

  • These are rules for building and adding on, so they matter most if a buyer plans an addition.
  • The presentation does not say whether a relief option for single-family homes was adopted, so ask the city before relying on it.
  • A person who disputes a hazard on a lot can submit a site-specific geologic report to the county geologist.

sections.h2: What is Mill Creek Canyon, and does it affect nearby homes?
sections.html:
Mill Creek Canyon is the national forest canyon just east of the city, close to the East Mill Creek and Mount Olympus neighborhoods. It is undeveloped and part of the Uinta-Wasatch-Cache National Forest.

Wikipedia's canyon entry lists a $5 per vehicle fee paid when leaving, a $50 annual pass, and seasonal limits, with the upper half closed to vehicles from November 1 through July 1. Dogs may be off leash on trails only on odd-numbered days, and must be leashed on even-numbered days. If you live near the canyon road, canyon traffic and trail parking are things a buyer may ask about.

sections.h2: Can a Millcreek house keep its accessory dwelling or rent it out?
sections.html:
Millcreek allows accessory dwelling units only on lots with an owner-occupied home, and the city records a notice on the title to say so. Because the notice stays on the title, a buyer's title company will see it.

  • Internal and attached units may be rented short term with an ADU application and a Millcreek business license. Detached units may not be short-term rentals.
  • Long-term rentals of 30 days or more are allowed in every ADU type with an ADU compliance letter and a business license.
  • Each unit needs at least one off-street parking stall, and a separate utility meter is not allowed.
  • A detached unit needs an R-1 or A zone, a lot of at least 8,000 square feet, up to 1,000 square feet of floor area and a rear-yard location.

Because the rules depend on owner occupancy, an investor who buys the house cannot assume the ADU stays rentable. If you built an unpermitted basement apartment, tell the buyer early.

sections.h2: Where do Millcreek residents shop, work and go to school?
sections.html:
Millcreek is mainly residential, with commercial development along Highland Drive, 3300 South and 3900 South, and a mixed-use area near Millcreek Common that combines housing, retail, restaurants and civic uses.

Granite School District fully serves Millcreek. It runs nine high schools, 15 junior highs and 62 elementary schools, with about 67,000 students in all, and Skyline High School is the one in Millcreek. The district was founded in 1904.

The Census Bureau puts mean travel time to work at 20.6 minutes.

sections.h2: How do Utah's primary residential exemption and tax calendar affect a Millcreek sale?
sections.html:
A Utah home that is someone's primary residence is taxed on 55 percent of its market value, and a second home is taxed on all of it. The state tax commission says the exemption requires 183 consecutive days of use as a primary domicile in a calendar year, and a household may claim only one.

The exemption does not automatically follow a sale, so a buyer who moves in files a new application. Applications go to the county Board of Equalization by September 15, and a late one can cost the owner the exemption for that tax year. The commission also says a landlord renting to a full-time tenant can claim it by submitting a declaration signed by every owner.

Under a 2026 change, owners must file Form TC-473A starting January 1, 2027 when ownership changes, including deed or trust transfers. The county's own calendar shows tax notices mailed by November 1, payment due without penalty on November 30, and delinquency on December 1.

sections.h2: How does a cash sale work for a Millcreek seller?
sections.html:
A cash sale in Millcreek lets you sell without a lender, an appraisal or listing prep. You describe the house, we make an offer based on its condition, and a title company handles the signing and the recording at the county.

Sellers often look at this route when a house has an unpermitted unit, a hillside lot with a long repair list or a probate delay.

faqs.q: When did Millcreek become a city?
faqs.a: Millcreek was incorporated on December 28, 2016, after voters approved it on November 3, 2015. It had been a county township since 2002.

faqs.q: Which school district serves Millcreek, Utah?
faqs.a: Granite School District fully serves Millcreek, and Skyline High School is the district's high school in the city. Confirm the zone for a specific address with the district.

faqs.q: Can I rent out an accessory dwelling unit in Millcreek?
faqs.a: Yes, if the lot has an owner-occupied home and the unit has a compliance letter. Detached units cannot be short-term rentals, but internal and attached ones can with an ADU application and a city business license.

faqs.q: What is the median home value in Millcreek?
faqs.a: The Census Bureau's 2020 to 2024 estimate for the median value of owner-occupied homes in Millcreek is $627,200. That figure describes the city as a whole and does not predict what your house would bring.

faqs.q: When are property taxes due in Millcreek?
faqs.a: The Salt Lake County Assessor lists November 30 as the last day to pay current-year real property tax without penalty. Unpaid taxes become delinquent on December 1.
